cycle_position.summary: Bifurcated by vintage: newly-built vacancy fell 480 bps YoY (Q1 2026, Cushman) while older-product vacancy rose 70 bps yet stays tight at 5.6%. IOS (industrial outdoor storage) is the momentum niche: sector sized ~$218B (up ~9% YoY), 2025 transaction volume $14-16B (+15-20% vs 2024), early 2026 tracking ahead. Improvement costs $15-40/SF vs $80-120/SF warehouse construction keep IOS yields attractive.

cap_rate_ranges.note: Widely reported tight but no clean 2026 cap-rate band captured this pass.

supply_demand.value: Older-stock vacancy 5.6% (tight); small-bay structurally undersupplied (nobody builds it — construction costs exceed achievable rents in most metros).

debt_terms.value: Local/regional bank recourse debt dominates the sub-$5M ticket; IOS financing products emerging (dedicated lenders advertise 65-75% LTV).

small_investor_verdict.entry_vehicle: Small IOS yards (1-5 acres, truck/contractor/equipment tenants) and older small-bay flex in secondary East Coast metros — the one industrial corner where $1-2M still buys a whole asset.
small_investor_verdict.reasoning: Yields (6.75-7.75%+ secondary IOS; 7-10% cash-on-cash) beat everything except the buyer's core 2-4 unit strategy, with NO residential-style rent regulation anywhere on the East Coast. Zoning is the moat and the diligence item: IOS lives or dies on by-right outdoor-storage use. Institutionalization is compressing primary-market yields — secondary metros (Richmond, Harrisburg, Allentown corridors) are where the small-buyer edge survives.

gaps: East Coast IOS/small-bay comps at the $1-2M ticket (portal-blocked; needs broker OMs)
Cold storage: institutional-scale only at this budget — not researched further
